_readme: A worked example of graded relevance judgements, over the documents that
already ship in config/eval/retrieval_corpus.jsonl. Copy it to
data/eval/retrieval_queries.json (which wins over the tracked default) and
replace the queries with your own -- the format needs no other change.
WHY THIS EXISTS. The shipped query set names exactly one relevant document
per query, which caps Precision@5 at 1/5 = 0.2 however good retrieval is.
P@5 there is not a retrieval result, it is a fact about the annotations, and
0.2 reads as a failure to anybody comparing it with a target quoted for a
multi-gold corpus. Supplying more judgements is what raises the ceiling;
improving the retriever cannot.
THE GRADES. 'relevance' maps a source identifier to a grade. Use the same
scale throughout a query set or nDCG compares two different things:
3  answers the question directly
2  answers part of it; a reader needs another document to be done
1  useful context, but cannot answer the question on its own
0  JUDGED AND NOT RELEVANT -- see below
GRADE 0 IS NOT THE SAME AS LEAVING A DOCUMENT OUT, to a human. To every
metric here the two are identical (_grades drops anything at or below zero,
so a 0 never counts toward recall and never enters the ideal ranking). What
it records is that somebody looked at that document and decided. That is
worth writing down for a document a retriever keeps returning: the next
person to read the file can tell 'we judged this and it does not answer the
question' from 'nobody has looked at this one yet'.
'expected_docs' STILL WORKS and can be used alongside. Anything in it that
'relevance' does not mention is graded 1. q-ex-04 below is written in the
old form on purpose, to show that a query set does not have to be migrated
all at once.
HOW MANY JUDGEMENTS. The ceiling for a query is min(relevant, 5) / 5, so
five relevant documents are needed before P@5 can reach 1.0. Do not pad to
get there. A judgement written to move a number is the one way this file can
make the measurement worse rather than better: mark a document relevant
because it answers the question, and let the ceiling be whatever falls out.
AND ANNOTATE THE NEAR MISSES. A corpus whose only documents are the answers
has nothing for precision to discriminate -- see the rows marked
'role': 'distractor' in the corpus, which exist only to be wrong.

_note: A broad question with three real answers: the entitlement, how to apply,
and what happens to unused days on departure. Ceiling 3/5 = 0.6.
The first two are graded 3 because either one answers a reader asking
this; the third is 2 because it answers a case, not the question.
chanjia.md is graded 0 rather than omitted: it is the document a lexical
retriever is most likely to return here (it shares 假), and writing the
judgement down means the next reader knows it was considered.
The narrow form of q-ex-01, and the pair is the point: the same three
documents, judged differently because the question changed. Ceiling is
back to 0.2 -- a narrow question has one answer, and no annotation
scheme can change that. This is what it looks like when a low P@5 is
correct.

queries.query: what do I need to know before claiming a meal expense
_note: Ceiling 3/5 = 0.6. The daily limit answers it; the approval threshold is
a 2 because a reader claiming a large expense needs it and a reader
claiming lunch does not; the accommodation standard is a 1 -- adjacent
policy, useful orientation, answers nothing on its own.
Note it is a Chinese document graded against an English query. That is
deliberate and it is a real case in a bilingual corpus: relevance is
about the content, not the script.

queries.query: how quickly is the on-call engineer paged
_note: The original ungraded form, unchanged. It is graded 1 automatically, so a
query set can be migrated a query at a time -- or never, if single-gold
is the truth for it.
